questions.q: Define "sectoral distribution of workforce" and state the formula for calculating the percentage share of the tertiary sector in total workforce.
questions.a: Sectoral distribution of workforce is the percentage breakdown of total employed persons across primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors. Tertiary sector share = (Workers in tertiary sector ÷ Total workforce) × 100. A wrong answer (e.g., using GDP shares instead of workforce numbers) reveals confusion between *output* contribution and *employment* contribution—a critical distinction because a sector can produce high output with few workers (high productivity) or employ many workers for low output (low productivity).

questions.q: Using Table 6.2 (2023–24), the primary sector employs 46.1% of the workforce but contributes only about 18% to GDP. Explain why this gap exists and what it implies for per-worker productivity in agriculture versus services.
questions.a: The gap exists because agriculture uses more labor per unit of output (labor-intensive, low capital, disguised unemployment), while services use less labor per unit of output (higher skill/technology). This implies per-worker productivity (GDP per worker) in primary sector is far lower than in tertiary. A student who says "primary sector is unproductive" misses the nuance: it is *low productivity per worker*, not zero productivity, and the gap signals surplus labor that could be redeployed.

questions.q: In 2023–24, India's total workforce was 545 million (from text). If the secondary sector share is 24.1%, calculate the absolute number of secondary sector workers. Then, using the 1972–73 secondary share of 10.9% and a 1972–73 workforce of 195 million (from Exercise 11), calculate the absolute increase in secondary workers over 50 years.
questions.a:
Step 1: 2023–24 secondary workers = 545 million × 24.1% = 131.345 million.
Step 2: 1972–73 secondary workers = 195 million × 10.9% = 21.255 million.
Step 3: Absolute increase = 131.345 – 21.255 = 110.09 million.
A wrong answer (e.g., using GDP shares or misreading the workforce total) shows inability to handle large-number arithmetic and percentage application—skills essential for board exam data-interpretation questions.

questions.q: Table 6.3 shows the secondary sector share stagnated at ~24% between 2011–12 and 2023–24, while the tertiary sector rose from 26.8% to 29.8%. Analyze why the secondary sector failed to absorb more workers despite "Make in India" and other industrial policies, and contrast this with the experience of East Asian economies.
questions.a: Stagnation reflects: (i) capital-intensive manufacturing growth (automation, skill-biased tech), (ii) labor law rigidities discouraging formal hiring, (iii) infrastructure/logistics bottlenecks raising costs, (iv) competition from cheaper imports. East Asia (e.g., Vietnam, Bangladesh) pursued labor-intensive export-oriented manufacturing, creating massive formal factory jobs. A student blaming only "lack of investment" misses the structural factors—technology choice, trade policy, and labor regulation—that jointly determine employment elasticity of manufacturing.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "India's rising tertiary sector workforce share (15% in 1972–73 to 30% in 2023–24) is a sign of successful structural transformation." Use evidence on job quality (self-employment, casualization) from Charts 6.1 and 6.2.
questions.a: The statement is only partially true. While the *share* rose, Chart 6.1 shows 54% of male and 67% of female workers are self-employed (mostly own-account, low-income), and Chart 6.2 shows urban casual wage labor is 12% (male) and 13% (female). Much tertiary growth is in low-productivity services (retail, transport, domestic work), not high-value IT/finance. A student agreeing fully ignores the *quality* dimension—structural transformation requires not just sectoral shift but movement into *regular, protected, productive* jobs.

questions.q: Construct a hypothetical scenario for a district where the primary sector workforce share falls from 60% to 40% over a decade, but the secondary sector share remains unchanged at 20%. Describe where the displaced primary workers likely go, what happens to their earnings and job security, and propose one policy to improve the outcome.
questions.a: Displaced workers likely swell the tertiary sector as informal self-employed (street vendors, gig workers) or casual labor (construction, loading), often with lower and volatile earnings, no social security. This is "premature deindustrialization" pushing workers into precarious services. Policy: Invest in labor-intensive manufacturing clusters (textiles, toys, food processing) with plug-and-play infrastructure, simplified labor compliance for new firms, and skill vouchers for displaced farm workers. A vague answer ("create jobs") fails to address the *sectoral* and *contractual* nature of the problem.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Sectoral distribution of workforce refers to the percentage distribution of a country's total workforce across the three major economic sectors—primary (agriculture, mining), secondary (manufacturing, construction, utilities), and tertiary/services (trade, transport, finance, public ______)—at a given point in time.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are visiting a village in Punjab where most families work on ______, and then you travel to Bengaluru where your cousin works in an IT firm and another drives for a ride-hailing app.
What is Sectoral distribution of workforce? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Sectoral distribution of workforce refers to the percentage distribution of a country's total workforce across the three major economic sectors—primary (agriculture, mining), secondary (manufacturing, construction, utilities), and tertiary/services (trade, transport, finance, public administration)—at a given point in time.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ask: "Why does primary still employ nearly half the workforce when its GDP share is below ______%?" This puzzle—low productivity per worker in agriculture—is the central economic principle: structural transformation lags behind output transformation.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Sectoral distribution of workforce?
questions.a: Students often equate "sectoral shift in workforce" with "sectoral shift in GDP" and assume a rising tertiary share automatically means rising per-capita income.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate sectoral workforce shares from raw employment data, interpret trends in sectoral shifts over multiple decades using Table 6.3, and explain the implications of a stagnant secondary sector share alongside rising tertiary share for labor productivity and job quality in India.
